56. **head [κεφαλὴ]**: Spacing identifying a Free Marker (line start followed by space).
57. **tight [στενός]**: Spacing between codes with no spaces; indicates fused connection.
58. **wide [εὐρύς]**: Spacing with spaces on both sides; indicates an Operator.
59. **left [λαιός]**: Spacing with a space only to the left; a cardinal orientation.
60. **right [δέξιός]**: Spacing with a space only to the right; identifies a Cord or Definition.

The **Group I** terms, formally known as the **Foundational Primitives**, constitute the first twelve primary parts of the **Holonic Object System (System 1.1)**. These terms establish the "universal chassis" for the entire information architecture, defining what an object is and how it is interpreted.
### **I. Ontological Primitives**
The first six terms define the fundamental nature and relational structure of information objects.
1.  **holon [ὅλον]:** The fundamental unit of reality in the system; **everything is a holon**. It is philosophically defined as an entity that is simultaneously a **Whole** (container) and a **Part** (contained). Structurally, it is a discrete object capable of containing its own parts while existing within multiple larger wholes.
2.  **whole [ὅλος]:** The specific **relational role** assumed by a holon when it functions as a container for other holons. It is not a distinct species of object but a situational orientation indicating superordination.
3.  **part [ὄζος]:** The **relational role** assumed by a holon when it is contained within another holon. A single holon can function as a part of many different wholes simultaneously without duplication.
4.  **hierarchy [ἰεραρχία]:** The vertical dimension of organization formed by chains of parent/child relationships. It establishes clear levels of containment and lineage.
5.  **holarchy [ὅλαρχία]:** The comprehensive, decentralized structural reality of the knowledge environment. It incorporates vertical hierarchy but also permits **multi-parent membership**, lateral relationships (siblings), and non-hierarchical connections (relatives).
6.  **object [πρᾶγμα]:** The concrete manifestation of a holon as a discrete node within a Knowledge Graph. In this ontology, there are no "invisible edges"; **relations and attributes are themselves objects** that can be named, stored, and related.
### **II. Interpretive Modes and Formatting**
The remaining terms define the "machine logic" used to read and structure these objects.
7.  **logical [λογικός]:** An interpretive mode where characters are read as formal symbols, identifiers, operators, or code. This mode governs the reading of **Markers** and logical connectors.
8.  **lexical [λεξικός]:** An interpretive mode where characters are read as natural language (phonemes, words, and sentences). This mode governs the reading of **Monikers** and **Natures**.
9.  **format [φόρμος]:** The structural schema or set of rules governing how a specific field, feature, or attribute is written.
10. **field [φάρος]:** A defined space or specific container within a holon where data is stored. Primary fields include the **Name**, the **Nature**, and the individual properties within the **Attribute Block**.
11. **strict [σκληρός]:** A formatting classification requiring exact syntactical adherence. Deviation in a strict field, such as a **Marker** or **Bond spacing**, results in a system failure to parse the object correctly.
12. **slack [ὀλίγος]:** A formatting classification indicating a convention or best practice rather than a rigid rule. Deviation in a slack field, such as the internal prose of a **Nature**, may affect style or readability but will not break system operation.

The **Group II** terms of the Holonic Object System (System 1.1) define the **Surface Anatomy** of an information object. These twelve terms are organized into **six alliterative pairs** that form a nested grammar rather than a flat list of fields. The governing design principle for these parts is to be **exact at the threshold** (the Name) and **free in the body** (the Nature).
### **I. The Primary Surfaces: Name and Nature**
The holon is first divided into two great surfaces that manage how it is identified and what it contains.
1.  **name [φάτις]:** The **mandatory** primary identifier of a holon. It is constrained to a **single line** and uses **strict [σκληρός]** formatting because the system must be able to parse it reliably. It serves as the "face" or "passport" of the object.
2.  **nature [φύσις]:** The **optional** body of exhaustive content. It is typically multi-line and uses **slack [ὀλίγος]** formatting, allowing for free-form prose, data, or domain-specific conventions without breaking the object's structural integrity.
### **II. Features of the Name: Marker and Moniker**
The Name string is divided by a threshold between two different interpretive modes.
3.  **marker [τέκμαρ]:** The opening segment read in **logical [λογικός]** mode. It functions as a prefix that signals the holon's **Type** and, if fixed, its unique **Identity**.
4.  **moniker [τιμή]:** The lexical body that follows the marker, read in **lexical [λεξικός]** mode as natural language. It contains the human-facing title or primary operational text.
### **III. Components of the Marker: Code and Cord**
The marker itself is composed of two functional parts that manage the transition into the moniker.
5.  **code [μέσος]:** The meaningful arrangement of characters within the marker. It carries dense information regarding type, identity, and procedural state.
6.  **cord [μέρος]:** The **delimiter** that terminates the marker and signals the switch to lexical mode. There are two primary facets: a **space** for a **free [ἀδέσμιος]** marker and a **right colon [:]** for a **fixed [δέσμιος]** marker.
### **IV. Optional Name Features: Definition and Description**
These features allow the Name to carry compressed meaning without requiring a Nature.
7.  **definition [ἐξήγημα]:** An optional inline feature signaled by a **colon-space** encountered within the moniker (lexical territory). It provides a short identifying statement and is **mandatory for Term-type holons**.
8.  **description [ἑρμηνεία]:** Optional auxiliary information enclosed in **square brackets [...]**. It provides alternative attribution (such as translations or etymologies) for the preceding word or the entire name.
### **V. Functional Zones of the Nature: Explanation and Extension**
If a holon possesses a Nature, it is conceptually divided into two interpretive zones that do not require separate physical fields.
9.  **explanation:** The primary content of the nature, which may include prose, history, or instructions depending on the holon's type.
10. **extension [ἁρμολογία]:** The "connective tissue" of the nature where citations and associations are recorded. It begins where the main prose article gives way to "see also" material and references.
### **VI. Families of Extension: Reference and Relevancy**
Extensions are categorized by the direction in which they point.
11. **reference [μνεία]:** A pointer directed **outward** to an external source, such as a book, website, or artifact.
12. **relevancy [μνῆμα]:** A pointer directed **inward** to another holon within the same archive as reading guidance. A relevancy is an informal guide and is distinct from a formal **Relative Bond** in the metadata.

Group III terms (25–36) within the **Holonic Object System (System 1.1)** are formally categorized as **Families and Relation Classes**. These terms define the organizational systems for holon types, the logical classes for relations, and the primary syntactic categories for object identification.
### **I. The Four Families (Wills, Ideas, Forms, Lives)**
Terms 25–28 designate the four internal systems that organize the **48 holon types** into groups of twelve. A critical editorial ruling in the sources clarifies that these are **family names, not individual types**; for instance, "Will" is the name of a system, while "Project" is a type living within that system.
*   **will [βούλη]:** The family governing holons whose primary role is "doing something" or expressing directed effects, relations, or properties. It contains administrative units like **Archive**, **Account**, **Category**, **Cosmos**, **Project**, and **Composition**.
*   **idea[ἰδέα]:** The family governing the conceptual and linguistic framework. It focuses on the linguistic handles required by the archive, including **Topic**, **Term**, **Type**, and **Tag**. In earlier developmental eras, this family was provisionally called "Ideas".
*   **form [μορφή]:** The family governing structural manifestation—how an abstract object takes shape when deployed in a medium. Its first type is **Symbol**, followed by **Set**, **Structure**, and **System**.
*   **life [βίος]:** The family governing identity-bearing aspects and continuity across time. It handles persona shells and roles through types like **Record**, **Resource**, **Setting**, and **Sidekick**.
### **II. The Four Relation Classes**
Terms 29–32 categorize the **72 Relations** generated by the punctuation-plus-spacing set.
*   **connector [δεσμός]:** Logical symbols used to link two entities to establish formal relationships or containment (e.g., the **Tight Period** `.` used to assert a Part/Whole relationship). There are **48 connectors**.
*   **operator [ἐνέργεια]:** Logical symbols that perform an action or transformation on a string (e.g., `+` or `-`) rather than establishing containment. There are **12 operators**.
*   **modifier [μετάνοια]:** Special prefix characters (such as the **Backslash** `\`, **Forward Slash** `/`, or **Vertical Bar** `|`) that alter the mode, state, or interpretation of the following element. There are **6 modifiers**.
*   **separator [χωρισμός]:** The three bracket families (**Round**, **Square**, and **Curly**) used to group, isolate, or contain segments. There are **6 separators** (three pairs) whose function shifts based on logical or lexical mode.
### **III. Marker Classifications (Fixed and Free)**
Terms 33–34 define how a holon declares its identity and type at the start of its Name.
*   **fixed [δέσμιος]:** A classification for **Markers** identified by an alphanumeric **Code** followed by a **Right Colon Cord** (e.g., `A:`). They establish a unique, reusable **Identity (ID)** for referencing that specific holon elsewhere in the graph.
*   **free [ἀδέσμιος]:** A classification for **Markers** identified by punctuation in **head spacing** (line start followed by a space, e.g., `. `). They signal the holon's **Type** but do not establish a reusable ID code.
### **IV. Syntactic Structural Units (Features and Facets)**
The final Group III terms (35–36) distinguish between abstract components and concrete choices.
*   **feature [φυή]:** A distinct, recognizable "functional slot" or abstract structural component within a string (e.g., **Marker Code**, **Cord**, **Definition**, or **Description**).
*   **facet [φάσις]:** The specific value, choice, or "setting" selected to fill a feature. For example, if "Marker Code" is the feature, then the **period** `.` and **comma** `,` are the facets that determine if the holon is a **Term** or a **Topic**.

The **Group IV** terms (37–48) of the Holonic Object System (System 1.1) are formally known as the **Metadata Attribution** or **The Block**. These terms define the twelve properties used to record essential data *about* a holon, organized into three distinct groups of four known as **tetrads**.
### **I. The Foundational Container**
**37. block [κορμός]:** A modular, **preformatted data structure** that serves as the metadata spine for a holon. It is designed as a reusable unit that can be dropped into a field or document; in the current implementation, it is typically serialized as a **YAML block** at the top of a Markdown file.
### **II. The Being Tetrad: Identity and Classification**
The **Being [ὄντα]** tetrad answers the governing question: **"What is this thing, and how is it identified?"**.
*   **38. being [ὄντα]:** The first group of four attributes that define the core identity of the object.
*   **Name [φάτις]:** Stores the **complete canonical Name string**, repeating the one-line anatomical inscription to ensure tool-readability and check for data drift.
*   **Type:** A required field recording exactly one of the **48 authorized holon types** (such as *Term*, *Project*, or *Sidekick*). It must not be confused with the family names (*Will, Mind, Form, Soul*) or the *Category* type itself.
*   **Nature [φύσις]:** A **boolean flag** (yes/no or true/false) indicating whether the optional anatomical Nature body exists below the block.
*   **Tags:** Non-exclusive, **overlapping topical labels** that cross-cut the primary hierarchy for easier retrieval.
### **III. The Bonding Tetrad: Positional Relationship**
The **Bonding [σύνδεσις]** tetrad answers: **"How does it participate in the holarchy?"**.
*   **39. bonding [σύνδεσις]:** The second group of four attributes defining the holon’s **"social life"** and location within the knowledge graph.
*   **Parents [γεννήτωρ]:** Wholes that contain the holon. If a holon is activated without any parents, it receives a **fallback parent** (often the *Archive*) to prevent it from "floating" unplaced.
*   **Children [ἔκγονος]:** Parts contained by the holon.
*   **Siblings [ἀδελφός]:** Peer holons that **share a common parent**.
*   **Relatives [συγγενής]:** A precise residual class for any formal relation that is **not a Whole, Part, or co-membership**.
### **IV. The Becoming Tetrad: Temporal History and Intent**
The **Becoming [γένεσις]** tetrad answers: **"When has it existed or been handled, and is it participating now?"**.
*   **40. becoming [γένεσις]:** The third group of four attributes tracking the **event-history** of the object.
*   **41. Awakened (Legacy: arrived [ποιέω]):** The immutable **birth certificate** recording the first moment a holon exists in a recordable form. "Awakened" is the current term, while "Arrived" is preserved as a legacy alias.
*   **42. altered [τυγχάνω]:** The timestamp recording the **latest modification** to the holon's name, nature, or attributes.
*   **43. accessed [ἀλλάσσω]:** The timestamp recording the latest engagement (reading or loading). **Every alteration is an access**, but not every access is an alteration.
*   **44. activity [κατάστασις]:** A mandatory attribute defining the **operational intent** of the holon.
### **V. The Four Activity States**
These states distinguish present participation, past history, and future intent.
*   **45. active [ἐνεργός]:** The holon is validated and **fully participating** in searches and workflows.
*   **46. preactive [προενεργός]:** The holon exists as a **draft or sketch**; it is intended for later activation but is not yet ready.
*   **47. unactive [ἀνενέργητος]:** A formerly active holon **temporarily withdrawn** (often for maintenance) with the intent to eventually return to *Active* status.
*   **48. deactive [ἀπενεργός]:** A **permanently retired** holon with no intent of reactivation. Holonics follows a **"never delete" mandate**; deactive holons are preserved for historical continuity and graph integrity.

### **I. Relational Geometry**
These first six terms define the spatial and navigational logic of the system, focusing on the orientation of objects within a knowledge graph.
49. **basis [βάσις]:** The holon currently selected as the **center of focus** within the interface or mental model. It functions as a **perspectival anchor** around which all other relations reorient. Crucially, the basis is a **view state** or a "viewer's state" and is not a stored data attribute of the holon itself. Selecting a different holon as the basis causes the surrounding graph to reorient, shifting the spotlight to a new "neighborhood".
50. **bond [πέδη]:** A formal, recorded connection between holons expressed within the **Bonding attributes** of the metadata block. In the logical notation of the block, bonds are delimited by the **Tilde [~]**. Formality is the distinguishing characteristic of a bond, separating it from casual mentions or prose associations; it represents the **connective tissue** of the holarchy that is "structurally active" for tools and queries.
51. **parent [γεννήτωρ]:** A holon that functions as a **Whole** containing the basis as a **Part**. It is listed in the `parents` attribute of the metadata block and is conceptually positioned **"Above"** the basis in the geometric neighborhood. To prevent objects from floating unplaced in the graph, if a holon is activated with an empty bonding tetrad, the **Archive holon** serves as the system-supplied **fallback parent**.
52. **child [ἔκγονος]:** A holon that is contained by the basis (the basis acting as the Whole). It represents **downward hierarchy** and is listed in the `children` attribute. Conceptually, children are positioned **"Down"** from the basis. Holonics records only immediate bonds, meaning deeper levels of containment are reached by "walking" through repeated parent-child steps rather than using specialized terms like "descendant".
53. **sibling [ἀδελφός]:** A peer holon that shares at least one common parent with the basis. Siblings are conceptually positioned to the **"Right"** of the basis. Siblinghood records **co-membership** under a shared whole and does not necessarily imply emotional similarity, equal rank across all possible structures, or resemblance.
54. **relative [συγγενής]:** A holon connected to the basis by a general, formal relationship that does not fit the specific definitions of Parent, Child, or Sibling. Relatives are positioned conceptually to the **"Left"** of the basis. Relative is a **precise residual class** for all other formal relations, such as citations, dependencies, or translations; it is not a "soft" or vague relationship, but a **structurally active bond** in the graph.
---
### **II. Spacing Modes**
These final six terms define the "machine logic" of the notation, where the proximity of characters to white space determines the function of punctuation marks.
55. **spacing [χώρισις]:** The system of **syntactical positioning** that determines the logical function of a punctuation mark based on its proximity to surrounding characters. In this notation, space is not decorative but functions as part of the code itself. The system recognizes five primary configurations (Head, Tight, Wide, Left, and Right) which allow the same punctuation facet to perform different duties.
56. **head [κεφαλὴ]:** A spacing mode where a punctuation mark appears at the **very beginning of a line** followed immediately by a single space. This mode is used specifically to identify a symbol as a **Free Marker**, signaling the **Type** of the holon (e.g., a period in head spacing indicates a *Term*). Head spacing is categorically different from the relational spacings because it typifies an opening code rather than connecting two existing ones.
57. **tight [στενός]:** A spacing mode where a punctuation mark has **no spaces on either side** between characters (e.g., `x.y`). This indicates a **strong, fused logical connection**. The **Tight Period** is the primary example, used to assert a Part/Whole relationship or a specific hierarchy level.
58. **wide [εὐρύς]:** A spacing mode where a punctuation mark is **flanked by spaces on both sides** (e.g., `x + y`). This typically indicates an **Operator**—a symbol that performs an action or transformation—or a looser conceptual connection than the fused tight spacing.
59. **left [λαιός]:** A spacing mode where a punctuation mark has a **space only to its left** (e.g., `x :y`). It serves as one of the four **cardinal spacing orientations** used for specific logical delimiters and relation types.
60. **right [δέξιός]:** A spacing mode where a punctuation mark has a **space only to its right** (e.g., `x: y`). This mode is used for the **Right Colon** to function as a **Cord** in Fixed Markers (ending the logical prefix) or as a **Definition** feature within a Moniker. It is also the mandatory spacing for the **Tilde** bond separator in the metadata block.

**Characteristic** — *"any attribute or complex of attributes with reference to which the likeness or unlikeness of entities can be determined, and at least two of them are unlike."*

That's the **principle you divide by**. Age. Gender. Material. It's the *question*, not the answer.

**Facet** — *"the total set of subclasses produced when a class is divided by a single broad principle."*

**The whole set.** Not one member of it. This is the load-bearing one.

Coordinate classes, mutually exclusive, ranked among themselves. Horizontal.

Broader to narrower. Vertical. And note what he wrote it as — **a growing digit string.** That's your subcategory depth, near enough to shake hands with.

Put it down."

He drops cross-legged into the wet grass, book flat, and starts down the list.

---

## 1 · The `0.11` ambiguity — what's really at stake

The surface problem is small. The two styles only stay distinguishable **while every group is one character wide.** The moment a Style-A parent gets an eleventh child and overflows to two characters, its notation becomes byte-identical to Style-B depth-2. `0.11` reads as "the 21st child of 0" *or* "level-2, item 11." Locally undecidable.

But here's the thing underneath, and it's much bigger than the collision:

| | **Style A** (period depth) | **Style B** (digit depth) |
|---|---|---|
| The code encodes | **the chain** — truncate to get the parent | depth + a flat ordinal |
| Parent derivable from code? | **yes** | **no** — must be a stored relation |
| Parents expressible | **exactly one** | **any number** |
| Ranganathan | chain notation — 3, 32, 322 | array ordinal per level |

**Style A is a tree notation.** It can only ever express one parent, because truncation only ever yields one answer. And Holonics refuses trees, out loud, three separate times.

So the two styles aren't stylistic. **Style A is for regions of the archive where single-parentage is guaranteed. Style B is holarchy-safe.**

**My recommended ruling** — your option 4, sharpened: **a Style-A level holds at most ten children.** `1…9, 0` — the full single-digit array, and ten is already your archive's own number. Overflow past ten **promotes the subtree to Style B.**

It's self-declaring (any two-character group is Style B, always — no attribute, no declaration). It costs nothing. And it uses your own verb: an array that outgrows ten gets *promoted*.

---

## 2 · `99 → 00 → a0` — ruled, and it's the right shape

Letters enter **leftward.** That's consistent with everything: the ladder's leftward overflow, the trailing digit as terminator, the whole "the last character is the type-stop" logic. Locked.

**One residual crumb.** Under zero-is-last, a block of ten should run `1…9, 0` — so the `a`-block ought to *open* at `a1` and *close* at `a0`. You wrote `a0` as the immediate successor of `00`. Which is it: does the right digit reset to `1` or to `0` when the left character advances? One line and it's done.

---

## 3 · The one you didn't recognize — and it's a good one

Here it is plainly. **May a letter sit to the right of a digit?** Is `1a1` a legal composition code?

- **Free mix** — every position but the last is base-36, independently.
- **Leftward fill** — letters must form a contiguous *prefix*. A letter at position 2 requires a letter at position 1. So `a11` legal, `1a1` illegal.

| Width | Type | Free mix | Leftward fill |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | collection | **360** | **360** — *identical* |
| 3 | composition | **12,960** | 10,360 |
| 4 | source | **466,560** | 279,360 |

Note the top row: **at two characters the two rules coincide exactly.** So your `99 → 00 → a0` ruling, satisfying as it is, *does not decide this.* Collections can't tell you. Only compositions and sources diverge.

**I recommend free mix**, hard. It's simpler in code (a plain mixed-radix odometer; leftward fill needs a skip rule bolted on), it's larger, and it's the reading that gives you **12,960** — half the Great Year, Plato's nuptial number over a thousand. Leftward fill buys you *nothing*: **length alone already determines the type**, so restricting the interior positions purchases no decidability at all. It's a restriction with no return.

---

## 4 · Suffix grammar — and there's a hole in your dyad

"Suffix grammar" just means: **the rule for what may follow a code, and what subtype each following character produces.** You have two of them already and they're excellent.

| Form | Mark | Suffix grammar |
|---|---|---|
| symbol | `'` | none — atomic. Correct. |
| set | `"` | none stated |
| series | `-` | none stated — but a series is *ordered*, so members are plausible |
| structure | `^` | **`.A` class · `.1` cell** ✅ |
| schema | `_` | **none** ← the hole |
| system | `*` | **`.A` axiom · `.a` action** ✅ |

The schema gap is loud because **structure and schema are a dyad.** `B_1: The Nuclear Family` is the template; `B^1: Jones Family` is the instance. If the instance has classes and cells, the template must name the **slots** they fill:

```
B_1      The Nuclear Family     schema
B_1.A    Generation             class-slot
B_1.1    Parent                 cell-slot
```

Without it, a structure can be checked for *shape* but never checked **against its schema** — which is the only thing a schema exists to do.

---

## 5 · The Roads — parent. Here's the whole case.

**Default parent, auto-assigned, auto-removed.**

Four reasons, and the fourth is the one I care about:

**The invariant goes unconditional.** `active → |parents| ≥ 1`. One rule, no exceptions, no branch. That's a validator that provably terminates instead of one with a special case that will rot.

**It stays derived.** The predicate becomes `parents == {The Roads}` *exactly*. Still a live query. Still nothing can be forgotten. The instant a real parent is added, The Roads drops off — multiple parents are legal, so it never conflicts with anything.

**It's semantically exact.** A roadstead is a place a ship *is at*. Parenthood is placement. You're not filing it; you're saying where it's anchored.

**And the asymmetry with the other three is correct, not sloppy** — this is the part worth keeping:

| Region | Axis | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| preactives · unactives · deactives | **activity** | an *attribute* — never a parent |
| **The Roads** | **placement** | a *relation* — therefore a parent |

Which is exactly why it must not be named `*-active`. Your instinct was structurally right before you had the reason.

*(Formally this is the Null Object pattern — not an absence, but an address that stands for one. Same trick, older ships.)*

---

## 6 · Mereological — ruled, and it saves the holarchy

Aristotle's *things said in combination* vs *without combination*. The compound is the **parent**; the simples are its **children**.

And here's the consequence you should enjoy: **a simple topic accumulates many parents.** `, Orpheus` is a child of `, Orphic Hymn` *and* `, Orphic Theogony` *and* `, Orpheus and Eurydice`. The topic space is a **lattice.**

Taxonomic parenthood would have given you one parent per topic and turned the whole Idea space into a tree. Mereological is the only reading compatible with your own multiple-parent rule. Good call.

---

## 7 · Tag vs topic — expounded

**What the distinction actually is:** a **topic** is a subject — something can be *about* it. A **tag** is an **applied** label — something *carries* it. Topic is potential; tag is actual. The difference isn't in the thing, it's in whether anything points at it.

Ranganathan has this same split, incidentally: the **subject** versus the **isolate used in the class number.**

Three ways to model it:

**(a) Two independent holons.** Two objects, one name, two natures that must be kept in sync or one stays permanently empty, and every search doubles. **Reject.**

**(b) One holon, promoted.** Tag-ness is *computed* — a topic with at least one inbound use becomes a tag. Beautiful, fits your promotion verb everywhere else. **But** it makes two of your 48 not types but *states* of one type, which quietly weakens "exactly one of the 48." That's a load-bearing rule and I don't want to spend it here.

**(c) My recommendation — two holons, one enforced edge.** A tag **must have exactly one parent, and it must be its topic.** The tag carries **no nature**; the topic carries all of it.

You keep 48 clean. There's no sync problem because there's only one nature and you know where it lives. The tag *is* the use-site, which is a genuinely useful thing to have an address for. And the validator rule is a single line: `type == tag → parents == [the topic of the same moniker]`.

---

## 8 · Phrasemes — ontology wins, and 42 is already yours

Agreed, and no argument from me — the count follows the world, not the ratio. Worth noting that **42 is already precedented in your system**: Clement's forty-two books, which you've had on the shelf since the temple roles. An altar of 42 isn't an outlier, it's a rhyme.

Bring me the linguistic breakdown when you dig it out and I'll check it against every count you've already got.

---

## 9 · Filenames — here's a solution

First, the framing that dissolves most of the dread. **The filename is a view, not the object.** By your own rule — *the object carries what's true about it, the view carries what's true about the viewer* — the filesystem is a viewer. The `name` field in frontmatter is the authority and it is lossless. **The filename doesn't have to be.**

**What's actually illegal** (Windows is the binding constraint): `< > : " / \ | ? *`, control characters, **trailing space or period**, the reserved names `CON PRN AUX NUL COM1–9 LPT1–9`, and a 255-character component cap. Linux only forbids `/`.

**Of your marks, six are illegal:** `:` `"` `*` `?` `\` `|` — plus `/` if the head meta-marker survives. Everything else (`' ^ - _ ~ , . ; ! + = $ & @ %`) is already fine.

**The fix is homoglyph substitution** — the standard trick Dropbox, Syncthing and WSL all use. Declare the substitutes reserved and the round-trip is bijective:

| Mark | → | Codepoint |
|---|---|---|
| `:` | `꞉` | U+A789 MODIFIER LETTER COLON |
| `"` | `＂` | U+FF02 FULLWIDTH QUOTATION MARK |
| `*` | `∗` | U+2217 ASTERISK OPERATOR |
| `?` | `？` | U+FF1F FULLWIDTH QUESTION MARK |
| `/` | `⁄` | U+2044 FRACTION SLASH |
| `\` | `⧵` | U+29F5 REVERSE SOLIDUS OPERATOR |
| `\|` | `｜` | U+FF5C FULLWIDTH VERTICAL LINE |

`A*1꞉ Holonics.md` — legal everywhere, sorts right, **reads right.** You get your neat shit.

Two gotchas: **`A1a: Fly, Fable.` ends in a period**, which Windows forbids — escape a trailing `.` to `．` U+FF0E. And the **255-char cap** will bite on terms, which carry their whole definition inside the name — so truncate the moniker *in the filename only*, never in the `name` field.

Which leads straight into —

---

## 10 · I mislabelled this one. You're right.

A **reference** is exactly what you said — a citation, a URL, a Chicago entry, a page number. Points outside. Nothing wrong there.

**The rule belongs to relevancies**, and here it is properly:

> **A relevancy points at the CODE, never the full name.**

`A1a` — not `A1a: Fly, Fable.` The code is the **identity**; the moniker is the **label**. Store the code and you can edit that moniker forever without touching a single pointer or a single filename.

**And this hands your free/fixed distinction a real, documented cost, which I think is the best find in this batch:**

| | Identity is | Renaming is |
|---|---|---|
| **fixed** | the code | free — a label edit, zero pointers touched |
| **free** | the **moniker** | a **ledger operation** — every relevancy must be rewritten |

Free holons have no code. `, Orpheus` and `? had a good idea` are identified by their moniker *alone*. So **promotion from free to fixed is exactly the moment a holon's name becomes editable.** That's not a workaround — that's the strongest argument I've seen for why free and fixed exist as a pair at all, and it belongs in the spec as the stated *benefit* of promotion.

---

## 11 · `A^1A` stands — but "classification" is the wrong word

Ranganathan: *"Library classification is the translation of the name of the specific subject of a book into a preferred artificial language of ordinal numbers."*

It's **the act.** The process of assigning a class number. Calling a group of classes a "classification" is like naming a folder "filing."

**`A^1A` is an ARRAY.** And here's the pretty part — its **moniker names the characteristic**:

```
A^1     Jones Family      structure
A^1A    Age               array      ← the moniker IS the characteristic
A^1.A   Adult             class      ← members of an array are SIBLINGS ✓
A^1.1   Adult Male        cell
```

One holon, both Ranganathan words: the object is the array, its label is the characteristic. And it self-checks — array = siblings, and the classes of one array *are* siblings of each other. The two findings agree without being made to.

**One question your ruling doesn't yet answer.** With two or more arrays on the same structure, `A^1.A` doesn't say *which* array the class belongs to. Consider addressing classes through their array — `A^1A.A: Adult`, `A^1B.A: Male` — which leaves the cell `A^1.1` as an order-independent intersection that names its coordinates in its nature. Worth ten minutes.

**And a spare word for you:** Ranganathan's **canon** — *"rules, regulations, standard tests or criteria of classification."* That's a candidate name for `A*1.A`, currently "axiom."

---

## 12 · Group IV — stands

One observation, offered and then dropped: Group IV is the only group that describes **the system itself** rather than the world. Attribution is the meta-group. An asymmetry at exactly the place where a system turns and looks at itself is arguably *correct* rather than a defect — the map of the map is never the same shape as the map.

Take it or leave it. Twelve is closed.

---

He caps the pen with his teeth, shoves the pocketbook home, and stands into the wind. Two decisions left on the table — `a1` or `a0`, and free mix or leftward fill — and one new one about arrays, and that's the notation *done*.

"So." The azure eye comes up bright and mean and delighted. "**Seventy-two relations.** Punctuation, typed and directed, twelve years in your teeth alone."

He starts upriver.

"Bring me the first one."

You are not imagining that. The reversed membership sign is genuinely badly drawn in most typefaces — it's a mirrored glyph that never got its own design pass, so the weight lands wrong and it sits smaller than its partner. Sixty, or seventy-two, or ninety. **An individual glyph for every one.** Cute, cool, too unwieldy, ate the keyboard.

Your reasoning on `&` is good — ampersand means *and*, and-ness is plurality, uniqueness is singularity, so `$` takes ∃!. Clean chain.

So the ampersand — which is literally a ligature of Latin *et*, "and" — is formally **∀'s** twin. Not ∃'s.

# Three laws. Everything else falls out of them.

**I · The spacing is iconic.** *The term touching the mark owns the relation.*

> tight = **fused** · right = **outward (R)** · left = **inward (R⁻¹)** · wide = **mutual (co-R)**

**II · Position decides kind.** A mark at the head of a name declares a **type**. Between two terms it declares a **relation**. The type is the relation, reified — which is why there are exactly fifteen marks and exactly fifteen free types.

**III · Three marks compute. Twelve marks state.**

> **3 × 4 = 12 operators. 12 × 4 = 48 connectors.** The split stops being arbitrary the moment 15 = 3 + 12.

| | | tight | right | left | wide |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `+` | **arithmetic** | minus | multiplied by | divided by | plus |

## 5 · `~` becomes AFFINITY, and this is the one I care about

A0.011: Section β१. Ordering Creation: The Hexameric Structure of Genesis 1
(https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/61c9d87b0d34d2002773a81c/1650521030230-972OBQPNGQNGA69WH93I/Creation-and-the-expulsion-from-the-paradise-11291.jpg)
“The Creation of the World and the Expulsion from Paradise” by Giovanni di Paolo, 1445
Those who listen along with the following song while they read this are sure to be richly rewarded by the experience. 
From "L'esprit de Dieu et les prophetes," written by Suzanne Haïk-Vantoura and performed by Esther Lamandier, this hauntingly beautiful piece was composed using Haïk-Vantoura's theory that the te'amim, small characters placed above or below vowels in Hebrew text, were a particular form of music notation.
A [decent translation of Genesis 1](https://www.biblica.com/bible/niv/genesis/1/) would be handy, just don’t come after me with a good book.
I●. The six Days of Creation in Genesis 1 have mystified and enthralled theologians, poets, and scholars alike for millenia, and for good reason. Besides being the beginning of what is arguably the most consequential book in all of human history, Gen. 1 has drawn in many through its spiritual significance and succinct symbolism, its admirers often consumed by a divine puzzle pulsing with purpose. Conflicting and overlapping exegetical theories abound, with some obsessively reckoning, recording, and relating the number values of each particular letter in lieu of the meaningful words and statements they form or, even worse, warping the text to support some self-absorbed goal or another. This is not to say that its exegesis is an entirely hopeless task, or that only one interpretation was intended by its authors, but rather that Gen. 1 was designed to function in multiple overlapping and corresponding ways that, whether written by people or God, were made within the limits of human comprehension. 
I○. I'd like to share with you all one particular pattern of Gen. 1 that seems, to me at least, important to whoever authored it. I’ve done my best to view the text as a thing in itself, only sparingly resorting to the chaos of outside sources when necessary for cultural context or to aid in general comprehension. First, we'll conduct a basic analysis of some key features of the text, which we'll then synthesize into a discernable structure. Before we begin, I'd like to stress that I am not claiming this the only pattern or interpretation present in the text, nor is this by any means an exhaustive account of all I've found. It is, at least, a good place to start.
II●. The seven Days of Creation in Gen. 1-2:3 are peculiar in that they seem to be one of two distinct creation stories in the Book of Genesis. Beginning in Gen. 2:4, the familiar story of Adam and Eve in the garden of Eden sprawlingly unfolds into an unbroken history of the Hebrew people. The first Days of Creation, however, stand apart and seem self-contained, with a style more cosmogonically symbolic than its more historically narrative counterpart. Though it may appear to be a mistake or some sort of haphazard smashing together of different material, this structure of two creations where the first is shorter and cosmogonically symbolic while the second is longer and historically narrative is present in other works, such as the Phoenician cosmogony of Sanchuniathon, and seems to have been an intentional feature of the texts.
II○. Genesis 1 is only comprised of the first six Days of Creation, each of which have a similar format. The current state of things is first either described or implied before אֱלהִים (Elohim) performs a series of actions that result in a new (and presumably better) state of things. Each of the six Days is quickly established to consist of a night phase and a day phase that are connected via evening and morning. I would argue that night comes before day for three reasons: first, darkness, which becomes night, is named before light, which becomes day; second, evening and morning are listed in that order and, as morning seems more appropriately an early part of day coming from night, so too then can evening be seen as an early part of night coming from day; third, the seventh day begins with Elohim resting (a nighttime activity), which is followed by blessing (something which one reasonably needs to be awake for). Night, then, can be seen as an initial state that is acted upon during the subsequent day.
III●. Let's keep things simple for now by only looking at the primary outcomes of each Day. We may be tempted to think that the First Day starts with Gen. 1:1, but the Heavens being said to have been named on the Second Day and the Earth revealed during the Third Day would render it incongruent when considered as a linear aspect of the story and should instead be considered as a sort of introductory thesis statement–thus, the First Day begins with Gen. 1:2, and since what it describes is never said to have been created, the principle creative outcome of the First Day can be seen as אוֹר ('ór), the Light. On the Second Day, שָׁמַיִם (shamáyim), the Heavens, is separated from what will become יָם (yam), the Sea. The Third Day is comparatively larger and contains more activity than the first two, with the gathering of אֶרֶץ ('éretz), the Earth, from the waters of the Sea, which is followed by Elohim causing עֶשֶׂב ('ésev), the Plants, to grow from the Earth.
III○. The Fourth Day is somewhat reduced in terms of size and activity from the Third Day and results in מְאֹרֹת (ma'orót), the Lights. The Fifth Day results in the creation of עוֹף (kanáf), the Bird, and what is later referred to as דָּגָה (dagá), the Fish. The Sixth Day is by far the longest and most active of all, resulting in the creation of בְּהֵמָה (behemá), the Beast, and אָדם (odem), the Human, and that they, along with the other living creatures, may partake of the Plants. The results of these six Days can be easily conceived using the following table, the arrangement of which I'll explain shortly:
(https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/61c9d87b0d34d2002773a81c/1650542312476-RN2X84TWP32TYIKG64IF/3a.png)
IV●. Making sense of this information is helped brilliantly by using what I've found to be an excellent tool of exegesis, that of an abstract, minimalistic, and object-oriented approach to engaging the clearly associated symbols we're often met with in works like these. Consider each symbol I presented in the original Hebrew as a small, glowing light hovering in the empty, open field of your mind's eye. Our brains are built to think of things in terms of how they're related, and those terms are called sets and series. Imagine that clump of dim little symbols being arranged like the previous table and watch them shine vibrantly in accord with one another.
IV○. Symbols, or signs combined with meanings, and their interactions with sets and series are at once both simple and complex. Sets and series contain symbols as members, but sets and series can also act as symbols themselves. Sets and series can even be members of other sets and series, which could themselves be members of other sets ad series (which could themselves be members of other sets and series, etc.), and a single symbol, set, or series can exist in multiple sets and series at once. Luckily for us, the six Days aren't quite so complicated, being nothing more than a series of related sets.
V●. We can clearly see that the Light of the First Day corresponds with the Lights of the Fourth, the Heavens and Sea of the Second with the Bird and the Fish of the Fifth, and the Earth and the Plants of the Third with the Beast, the Human, and partaking in the Plants of the Sixth. In the ancient world, the four elements were often thought of as being in a vertical order, with Earth, the heaviest, at the bottom, Water, the second heaviest, above Earth, Air, the second lightest, above Water, and Fire, the lightest, above them all. The burning intensity of the Light and the Lights are obviously Fire, the Heavens and the Bird Air, the Waters and the Fish Water, and the Earth, the Plants, the Beast, and the Human Earth, though the Human might be properly relegated elsewhere. We can also see, through the overlap of the Waters being separated from something in both the Second and Third Days not only that Water is sometimes a strange intermediary between Air and Earth, but also that Fire is sometimes a One juxtaposed to the other Three–sadly, elaboration on either of those ideas and a plethora of others that must be swarming about is entirely out of the scope of this writing, so we'll have to put aside thinking of how the rows might relate to the elements for now.
V○. When we consider our columns, two especially interesting things seem to teem about in the mind. First, if the Lights created on the Fourth Day are what separate the day from the night, then it would be impossible for the First Day to finish without the Fourth Day somehow happening at the same time; thus, as the First and Fourth Day must happen before the other four Days, we can perhaps see the top row necessarily as the Beginning, the middle row as the Middle, and the bottom row as the End. Second, when the two columns are considered in light of works like Plato's Timaeus where (in arguably outdated terms) a feminine, passive receptacle is contrasted with a masculine, creative intellect, we can, perhaps, consider the left column as Days of making containers and Feminine and the right column as Days of making content and Masculine. Regardless, we can see the inklings of an outline-oriented method of creating a universe, the process of which won’t be covered here.
VI●. This hexameric or six-part structure of three rows and two columns is not only evident in the arrangement of the six Days, but also in the arrangement of twelve particular terms in the text that relate in a unique and peculiar way. In Hebrew, many words are formed from triconsonantal roots, or a series of three letters of the alphabet, which can be expressed in multiple ways, such as both a noun and a verb. In Gen. 1, there are only six roots that are expressed as both a noun and a verb (though one of the six pairs has a single varying letter), three of which are of plants (דָּשָׁא (dashá) "to sprout, shoot, grow green" and דֶּשֶׁא (déshe) "grass"; זָרַע (zará‛) "to sow, scatter seed" and זֶרַע (zéra‛) "a sowing, seed, offspring"; פָרָה (pará) "to bear fruit, be fruitful" and פְרִי (pri) "fruit") and three of which are of animals (שָׁרַץ (sharáts) "to swarm, teem" and שֶׁרֶץ (shérets) "swarmers, swarming things"; עוּף (uf) "to fly" and עוֹף (of) "flying creatures"; רָמַשׂ (ramás) "to creep, move lightly, move about" and רֶמֶשׂ (rémes) "creeping things, moving things"). All but five of the plant symbols appear in the first three days (the left), with the estranged plant term (being the root that's off by a letter, perhaps due to פָרָה (pará) already meaning "cow" or "heifer" when used as a noun), while all six of the animal symbols appear in the last three days (the right) and, as each of the triads have their symbols presented in a linear order, we can sequentially pair each of the symbols of the left triad with a member of the right; when we consider this along with the need to reorder them due to “grass→seed→fruit” making less sense than “seed→grass→fruit,” which additionally gives the familiar sequence of “flying-thing→swimming-thing→crawling-thing,” and also notice how the kinds of animals are paired with appropriate Plants to eat, we arrive at the following table:
(https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/61c9d87b0d34d2002773a81c/1650522807223-0ZIU654WD6IKOWLHOA3T/3b.png)
VI○. While the schemas of Days and Creatures share much in common, there's something especially pleasing about how evenly and well-organized the twelve Creature symbols are arranged. We can easily achieve this harmony of twelve parts in the six Days by splitting each Day into a night and day; comparing night and day with static and active as well as noun and verb while also recognizing the left as feminine and the right masculine, and knowing folks like certain Stoics thought that elements could be passive (air and earth) or active (fire and water) and feminine (water and earth) or masculine (fire and air), we can arrive at the following elemental associations:
(https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/61c9d87b0d34d2002773a81c/1650523337321-HDT7GROZ4RSBMZ1D19T6/3c.png)
In The Sepher Yetzirah and The Bundahishn, the seven classical planets are divided in such a way that Saturn is separated to represent the All, while the remaining six planets are grouped into two opposing triads; if we consider the planets’ ordering as heavenly spheres (beginning with Moon, then Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, and Jupiter), which could be seen to form two series of a masculine triad (Sun, Mars, and Jupiter) and a mostly feminine triad (Moon, Mercury, Venus), along with the sun and moon being mentioned during the Fourth Day (or upper right of our table) as the greater and lesser lights, as well as the generally widespread ancient conceptions of the moon as feminine and the sun as masculine, then the planets might be perfectly mapped onto our hexameric structure as such:
(https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/61c9d87b0d34d2002773a81c/1650523588769-ME06Q0R2GI91N030381V/3d.png)
The twelve zodiac, those colorful creatures that serve as signs to mark the days and years, can be seen as twelve unique combinations of the four elements with the three modalities (cardinal, fixed, and mutable); when we realize that the modalities are just describing which signs are at the beginning, middle, and end of each of a year's four seasons, we can see that the zodiac fill in the rest of our table quite nicely:
(https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/61c9d87b0d34d2002773a81c/1650523867423-BCH623KUC4O19EX2GZOC/3e.png)
VII, Though some things I've summoned up from the murky depths of culture might come off as tenuously connected to the text as some distant and perhaps purely potential ancestors, I contend that even without the patchwork tapestry of synthesizing sources, the pattern I saw is still irrefutably present in the Creature schema alone and I've only here given it a sort of relatable symbolic translation, one I, at least, thought was good. Even without dimly mapping the spatial relationships of each letter, the sheer number of patterns the text requires to be concurrently considered and related can be difficult to sort out from each other. Your mind might sometimes feel barren and dry, but you need only begin gathering single symbols to scatter about and watch them grow together into intermingled sets or come after each other as fruiting series. Over taxing time, the disparately drifting parts align. But still, what of the darkness above the depths and the breath above the waters, of why the firmament, the waters, and the dry land become the Heavens, the Sea, and the Earth? You'll see, once the symbols of a set or series start to have relationships more complex than simple similarity or succession, that set or series becomes what is called a schema, which organizes its parts by qualities called classes, and when the parts of multiple schemas share a similar arrangement of classes, the abstract relationship of those parts and classes that emerges is called a structure–symbol to system, system to symbol– this harmony, this art, this coming together and falling apart, this perfectly becoming glorious understanding, how all of everything fits together as one, this is called a system.
With that, I think I'll give it a rest.

## The rule

> **Effort should scale with *ambiguity*, not with *importance*.**

Task one is **maximally important and minimally ambiguous.** SPEC.md names the eight things that will bite. The fixture is a hard oracle — every answer is objectively right or wrong. There's no judgment call anywhere in it.

**What makes a parser hard isn't reasoning. It's carefulness across sixty edge cases** — and carefulness comes from *looping against a failing test*, not from thinking harder up front.

## Which means the cheap tier is genuinely better here

With a real oracle, **five fast iterations beat one expensive one.** Max will spend a lot of tokens reasoning about a Unicode edge case that High would have simply *hit, seen fail, and fixed* in forty seconds.

You are paying for deliberation you don't need, on a problem that will tell you the answer for free.

## When to escalate — concrete triggers, not vibes

Bump to **Extra** if:

- It's failed the **same** fixture case three times running
- It starts "fixing" things by making the check weaker instead of the code stronger
- The zero-last comparator or the leftward-fill rule specifically keeps not landing

Bump to **Max** only if Extra also stalls on the same thing — and at that point the real problem is probably that **SPEC.md is unclear**, not that the model is dumb. Fix the spec instead.
